subject: Cooking
title: The Emperor's Falling Leaf: Tea's Origin Story
description: A quick, practical guide to The Emperor's Falling Leaf: Tea's Origin Story.

hook.text: Chinese legend says Emperor Shennong discovered tea in 2737 BCE when a leaf fell into his boiling water.

buildup.text: Tea cultivation began in China's Yunnan province — ancient tea trees there are over 3,000 years old.

discovery.text: Tea was first used as medicine, then as a Buddhist meditation aid, before becoming a daily beverage.

twist.text: All tea — green, black, white, oolong — comes from the same plant: Camellia sinensis. Processing creates the variety.

climax.text: Tea is the second most consumed beverage on Earth after water — 3.7 billion cups are drunk daily.

punchline.text: One leaf in hot water. 5,000 years of culture followed.

quiz.question: How many types of tea plant produce all varieties of true tea?

details.summary: Chinese legend credits Emperor Shen Nung with discovering tea in 2737 BCE when wild tea leaves blew into his pot of boiling water. The pleasant drink that resulted launched a tradition spanning five millennia.
details.whyItMatters: Tea is the most consumed beverage after water, drunk by over two billion people daily. Its Chinese origin story connects the modern habit to five thousand years of cultural history.
takeaways: Legend places tea discovery at 2737 BCE with Emperor Shen Nung
Tea comes from the Camellia sinensis plant native to China
Over two billion people consume tea daily worldwide

faq.question: Are all types of tea from the same plant?
faq.answer: Yes. Black, green, white, oolong, and pu-erh all come from Camellia sinensis. The difference is processing — oxidation level, heat treatment, and rolling technique. Green tea is minimally oxidized. Black tea is fully oxidized. Oolong is partially oxidized.

faq.question: When did tea become widely consumed in China?
faq.answer: Tea consumption became widespread during the Tang Dynasty from 618 to 907 CE, when Lu Yu wrote the Classic of Tea. Before that, tea was primarily medicinal. The Tang court popularized tea drinking as a refined practice. By the Song Dynasty, it was central to Chinese daily life.
